posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring ICP post with three ideal prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain point and add the 'explainability vs. output' distinction without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' problem is exactly it. Most AI analytics tools optimise for getting you an answer fast — almost none of them are built to show the working. And in financial services, the working IS the answer. Curious whether your team is still looking for something that can fill that gap or has just gone back to manual for now?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consultancy hitting the adoption wall with Power BI — validate the trust problem specifically, not just the change management cliché
posts.draft_comment: The Excel thing isn't stubbornness — it's that your finance team has been burned before by a number that looked right but wasn't, and they're not going to stake their reputation on a dashboard they didn't build. 18 months of engineering doesn't buy that trust. Honestly, what was the last number from Power BI they *did* quote confidently, and what made that one different?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post that validates dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why it happens' layer, leave Claire thinking
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is actually pretty restrained — I've seen ops teams with north of 200. The real issue is that dashboards get built to satisfy the person who asked for the dashboard, not the person who has to act on it. Those are almost never the same person. Makes you wonder how many 'data-driven' decisions are really just gut calls with a chart attached.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI failure — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the missing layer about definitions not being a tooling problem
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so familiar it's almost a rite of passage. But I'd push back slightly on the framing — the problem usually isn't that people built too much, it's that nobody defined what 'right' looked like before they handed out the licenses. Governance conversations feel boring until you're six months in and your CFO is querying which revenue number to use in an investor call. Who owns the truth is exactly the right question — just worth asking it before the rollout, not after.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucination as a material risk with a CEO prospect engaged — validate the reframing from accuracy to trust/security, add the specific compounding risk that gets missed
posts.draft_comment: The reframe from accuracy issue to security issue is the right one — and I'd argue it's even more specific than that. The real danger isn't the hallucinated number itself, it's that it looks exactly like a real one. No error message, no red flag, just a clean report that someone screenshots into a board deck. How many organisations even have a review step between 'AI generated this' and 'we're acting on this'?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP-adjacent CEO venting about the exact pain Milo solves, with a COO in the thread — validate the '£200k paperweight' reality with a sharp observation about who BI is actually designed for
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number stings but it's not even the real cost — it's the 18 months of 'just send me the dashboard' emails that follow. Most BI tools are basically built so a data analyst can feel productive, not so a ops or finance person can actually answer their own questions on a Tuesday morning. The self-service label has become a way to shift the blame onto the user when the tool fails. How many of those £200k installs do you reckon are genuinely used by more than two people?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely mid-market industrial company has surfaced a classic data trust problem — validate the root cause (governance, not AI), add the cultural layer with a sharper edge
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, one dataset, three answers — that's not a data problem, that's a 'who owns the definition of revenue' problem. And no amount of AI summarisation fixes it if nobody's agreed what the number even means before the dashboard loads. The culture piece is real, but in my experience it usually needs one person willing to have a very boring, very important meeting about filter logic. Did your CFO leave that review trusting the dashboard more, or less?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with enterprise AI — validate the 'nobody knows what to ask' insight and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tooling problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me at all. The gap isn't the tool being bad — it's that most people don't have a clear enough mental model of their own data to know what question would actually be useful to ask. Shadow AI on phones is the symptom, not the problem. What does the 12% who stuck with it actually have in common?
